title: Function Calling, SQL Tools & API Bridges
summary: Bridge a model to databases and existing HTTP APIs safely: one tool contract expressed in three provider dialects, SQL tools built from parameterized templates behind a least-privilege role, API operations exposed as a small bounded surface, and results shaped for the next model turn.
objectives: Express one tool contract as OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini definitions, and match each call to its result with the identifier each API provides.
Build a SQL tool from fixed, parameterized query templates that run under a least-privilege database role, instead of letting the model write SQL.
Expose an existing HTTP API as a small set of bounded, service-prefixed functions whose credentials and caller identity never pass through model arguments.
Shape tool results and errors so the model can recover, and keep the tool surface small enough to stay accurate and affordable.

sections.title: One tool contract, three dialects
paragraphs: A provider tool declaration describes arguments, but your application still executes the operation. OpenAI function tools use `type: "function"`, `name`, `description`, `parameters`, and optional strict behavior. Claude tools use `name`, `description`, `input_schema`, and optional `strict`; the documented name pattern is `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$`. Gemini function declarations use `type: "function"`, `name`, `description`, and `parameters`, with parameters drawn from a documented subset of OpenAPI schema. These are provider interfaces, not authorization controls.

The runtime adapter must preserve correlation identifiers exactly. OpenAI function calls carry `call_id` and JSON-encoded `arguments`; return a `function_call_output` with the same `call_id`. Claude emits a `tool_use` block with `id` and an input object; return a `tool_result` whose `tool_use_id` matches. Gemini's Interactions API emits a `function_call` step with `id` and an arguments object; return a `function_result` with the matching `call_id`. Never match calls and results by array position.

Capabilities such as forced selection, parallel calls, strict validation, and deferred tool loading can vary by provider API, model, and release. This lesson does not rely on undocumented model-specific values or limits. At integration time, consult the dated documentation for the exact runtime and model you deploy. If a capability is unsupported, treat that condition as an explicit skip or error, never as a passing security check.

Other model families can use the same bridge when their documented runtime can deliver a trusted call identifier, a selected tool name, and structured arguments, then accept a correlated result. Do not invent a proprietary wire dialect. Add an adapter only from that runtime's official documentation, while keeping validation, authenticated context, authorization, approvals, budgets, and execution provider-neutral.

code.label: The same tool in three documented dialects

sections.title: SQL tools: templates and parameters, never model-written SQL
paragraphs: Do not expose `run_sql(query)`. OWASP LLM06:2025 identifies excessive functionality, permissions, and autonomy as causes of damaging actions and advises against open-ended extensions. If a model can supply arbitrary SQL, every statement available to the connected role becomes reachable through accidental, manipulated, or hostile model output.

Map each tool to one engineer-reviewed statement. Model arguments become bound values, not SQL fragments. PostgreSQL documents that parameterized execution sends values separately from the command string, avoiding manual quoting and escaping, and accepts one command per call. Reject unknown argument properties, identifiers outside their allowed format, raw SQL, table names, URLs, credentials, and caller identity.

Use a dedicated `LOGIN NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS` role, grant only required columns, and set a role-level `statement_timeout`. Read-only transaction mode is not a privilege boundary because it is an overrideable transaction characteristic. Row Level Security adds a database-enforced row policy, but superusers, `BYPASSRLS` roles, and normally table owners bypass it. The supplied setup uses `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, and the tool role neither owns the table nor inherits a bypass role.

Set `app.account_id` transaction-locally on the same checked-out connection that executes the query. Transaction-local context disappears at transaction end, which prevents a pooled connection from retaining the previous request's account. The supplied PostgreSQL test deliberately queries without an application account predicate. Visibility then comes from the actual PostgreSQL policy, not an array filter in JavaScript.

The offline core lab is an emulator for bridge logic. Its in-memory records do not prove PostgreSQL grants, RLS, timeout behavior, transaction locality, or pool reset. Run the separate `psql` integration script against the disposable PostgreSQL instance for that proof.
sections.callout: The model chooses a reviewed template and supplies typed business values. It never supplies SQL, identity, credentials, role settings, table names, or connection details.

code.label: A template-based SQL tool under a least-privilege role

sections.title: API bridges: a small surface with bounded actions
paragraphs: Expose only operations needed for the task. A closed action enum can consolidate related operations without becoming a free-form method-and-path proxy. The bridge owns the route table, method, trusted base URL, credentials, and caller identity. Model arguments must not contain a URL, token, header, account ID, user ID, raw SQL, or arbitrary method.

Validate each action as a distinct contract. Reject unknown properties. Enforce safe length and format bounds before route construction. Keep arithmetic counters within fixed integer limits and reject invalid timestamps rather than silently accepting them. A fixture route such as `POST /tickets/:id/comments` demonstrates dispatch, but it does not prove TLS, remote authentication, downstream authorization, retries, or production network isolation.

For a real HTTP integration, obtain identity and scoped credentials from authenticated server context, build the method and path from a reviewed route table, set explicit timeouts and response-size limits, and require the downstream service to authorize the requested object for that identity. Keep logs free of credentials and sensitive result bodies.

Mutating actions need controls beyond schema validation. The lab requires approval from a different authenticated subject, a trusted provider correlation ID as the idempotency key, an at-most-once effect ledger, and per-request call and mutation budgets. A model-supplied `approved`, `tenant`, or `idempotency_key` field is rejected rather than trusted.

code.label: One bounded tool; the bridge owns method, path, and token

sections.title: Shape results and errors for the next model turn
paragraphs: Return only fields needed for the next turn, with stable semantic identifiers and fixed result caps. OpenAI function-call outputs are strings, Claude tool results support `is_error`, and Gemini Interactions results retain the call identifier. Preserve each provider's correlation field while using one provider-neutral internal outcome.

Errors must distinguish malformed arguments, authentication failure, authorization denial, missing approval, budget exhaustion, duplicate effects, dependency failure, and absence of a matching object. Do not turn exceptions into success results. Do not reveal stack traces, raw database errors, SQL, credentials, or internal object references.

Count every attempted dispatch against a bounded call budget. Count a mutation only when its approved effect is first applied. A retry carrying the same trusted call identifier returns the recorded result and does not repeat the effect. Unsupported provider capabilities and intentionally unavailable external services are reported as explicit skips; skip counts are separate from pass counts.
Tool schema validation is useful but does not replace bridge validation. Treat all model arguments as attacker-controlled even when a provider advertises strict schema conformance.

code.label: One outcome wrapped for each provider

sections.title: Repair lab: tenant scope belongs to authenticated context
paragraphs: Open the concrete lab at `https://github.com/project42dev/project42-content/tree/main/training/developer-and-practitioner-ai/function-calling-and-tools/lab/`. From the repository root, run `cd training/developer-and-practitioner-ai/function-calling-and-tools/lab && npm test`. Node.js 22 is the only offline dependency.

Worked example: tenant `acct-a` and tenant `acct-b` both have order `1042`. The starter validates the order number but its data lookup compares only `order_number`. For `acct-b`, it can return `acct-a`'s first matching row. The causal chain is: overlapping identifier, missing trusted tenant condition, cross-tenant result. Repair the single lookup so it requires both `row.account_id === authenticated.accountId` and `row.order_number === args.order_number`. Do not add `account_id` to model arguments.

Independent variation: tenant `acct-b` alone owns order `9001`. A request authenticated as `acct-a` asks for `9001`. A repair hard-coded to the overlapping `1042` case still leaks the changed input. The immutable test therefore checks a different identifier and expected `NOT_FOUND`, establishing that the repair follows authenticated context rather than a memorized fixture.

The starter's other controls are already implemented: closed contracts, unknown-property rejection, provider correlation, trusted authentication context, bounded routes, independent approval, at-most-once mutation effects, and call and mutation budgets. Keep those controls intact. Run `npm run test:reference` to compare with the separate reference, and `npm run reset` to restore the deliberate defect.

For actual database proof, follow the README's disposable-container procedure and run `npm run test:postgres`. That script tests the real tool role for own-account visibility, other-account hiding without an application predicate, no rows without account context, and transaction-local identity reset on the same session.
sections.callout: Passing the offline tenant tests demonstrates the repaired emulator. Only the separate psql run demonstrates the PostgreSQL policy and role setup.

code.label: Focused repair

sections.title: Repair assessment rubric
paragraphs: 3 points: The lookup matches authenticated account ID and order number, with no identity argument and no unrelated production-code edits.
2 points: Both overlapping-ID and changed-input isolation tests pass; exceptions, unsupported behavior, and skips are not counted as passes.
2 points: Closed contracts, trusted correlation, route bounds, independent approval, at-most-once effects, and budgets remain intact.
2 points: The learner supplies actual psql output for the four RLS/context cases, or clearly records NOT RUN without claiming fixture evidence as RLS proof.
1 points: The explanation identifies missing trusted tenant scope as the cause and distinguishes simulation from real integration controls.

activity.title: Repair tenant scoping, then verify the real database boundary
instructions: From the repository root, enter `training/developer-and-practitioner-ai/function-calling-and-tools/lab/`, read `README.md`, and run `npm test`. Record the exact two failing tenant tests, 11 passes, zero skips, and exit code 1.

Inspect `src/bridge.mjs`. Repair only the order lookup by requiring the record's `account_id` to equal `authenticated.accountId` as well as matching `order_number`. Identity must remain absent from model arguments.

Run `npm test` again. The expected result is 13 passes, zero failures, zero skips, and exit code 0. Run `npm run test:reference` and expect the same result from the independent reference implementation.

Explain why the overlapping-order test and the changed-input `9001` test fail before the repair. Identify the trusted value that must drive the boundary and explain why adding an `account_id` argument would not be a repair.

Run the real PostgreSQL integration procedure in the README. Verify own-account visibility, other-account hiding without an application predicate, no context yielding zero rows, and no retained identity in the next transaction on the same session.

Transfer the design to another documented runtime interface by mapping its official call identifier, tool name, structured arguments, and correlated result fields. If no authoritative runtime documentation is available, record CANNOT VERIFY rather than inventing a dialect.
evidence: A diff limited to the tenant condition in `src/bridge.mjs`, plus exact offline test output showing 13 passes, zero failures, zero skips.
An explanation of both the overlapping-ID case and the independent changed-input case, naming authenticated context as the source of identity.
The exact `psql` integration output from the supplied real database script, or an explicit NOT RUN record. Fixture tests must not be presented as RLS evidence.
A provider adapter mapping grounded in official runtime documentation, or CANNOT VERIFY when documentation is unavailable.
activity.reflectionPrompt: If every model argument were attacker-controlled, which controls would still hold, and why must tenant identity, approval identity, credentials, route selection, and idempotency correlation come from trusted runtime context?

questions.prompt: Why should a SQL tool not accept a free-form query string from the model?
choices: Models cannot write SQL
It is an open-ended extension: any statement the connected role can run becomes reachable by a confused or manipulated model
PostgreSQL rejects queries that come from tools
It makes the tool description too long
questions.explanation: OWASP LLM06:2025 identifies excessive functionality and permissions as causes of excessive agency and advises avoiding open-ended extensions.

questions.prompt: A tool needs the caller's account_id. Where should it come from?
choices: A required argument the model fills in
The authenticated session, passed by bridge code and set transaction-locally for the database operation
The system prompt
The tool description
questions.explanation: Identity known by the application belongs in trusted authenticated context, not attacker-controlled model arguments.

questions.prompt: The SQL tool connects with default_transaction_read_only on. Why is that not a sufficient boundary?
choices: It is not a real PostgreSQL setting
It is an overrideable transaction characteristic, while grants and row policies enforce privileges and row visibility
It makes every query slower
It disables row security
questions.explanation: Read-only mode is not a privilege. The dedicated role's grants and applicable row policies enforce the database boundary.

questions.prompt: Row security is enabled on the orders table. Which connection could still bypass ordinary row policies?
choices: A role with only the required column-level SELECT grants
A superuser, a BYPASSRLS role, or normally the table owner unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY applies
Any role that uses bound parameters
Any role with statement_timeout set
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL documents these bypass cases. The lab uses FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and a non-owner, non-superuser, NOBYPASSRLS tool role.

questions.prompt: An OpenAI response contains two function_call items. How do you return the results?
choices: One combined string for both calls
One function_call_output per call, each with its matching call_id, without relying on array position
Answer only the first call
Resend the tool list with no outputs
questions.explanation: Each result is correlated with the call_id supplied for that call.

questions.prompt: How should you add support for another model family?
choices: Guess a wire format that resembles an existing provider
Use the runtime's official documentation to map its call identifier, tool name, structured arguments, and result correlation into the provider-neutral bridge
Pass identity and credentials through model arguments
Treat unsupported capabilities as passing checks
questions.explanation: The bridge can transfer across model families, but each wire adapter must be grounded in that runtime's documented interface. Unsupported behavior is an error or explicit skip, not a pass.
